turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels, process/composition
    columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B, Al, Cu, W, S, Heat
    treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment
    step 1 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment
    step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2 cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3
    temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3 cooling
    rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1
    time, Secondary treatment step 2 temperature, Secondary treatment step 2
    time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4
    time, Thermal exposure temperature, Thermal exposure time) and the two
    measured objectives `yield strength (MPa)` and `elongation (%)` (both at
    room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose objectives were
    NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same process/composition
    columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH elongation (%). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), elongation (%)) plane, so a set of
mutually non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates
that are all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would select a **frontier-spanning set**, using composition-and-treatment analogues in the training data rather than ranking candidates by strength alone.

| Candidate | Intended frontier role | Training-data support |
|---|---|---|
| **c018** | High-elongation anchor | Its composition and primary treatment match a training steel measured at **278 MPa, 62% elongation**. The additional thermal exposure introduces uncertainty, but it remains a strong ductility-side choice. |
| **c051** | Ductility-rich intermediate | A nearly identical steel, solution-treated at 1150°C rather than 1100°C, achieved **375 MPa, 53% elongation**—a useful strength increase over the ductility anchor. |
| **c012** | Middle-frontier balance | The same composition achieved **700 MPa, 34% elongation** under a different solution-and-aging schedule. This supports its potential to bridge the ductile and high-strength regions, although its changed treatment makes the prediction less certain. |
| **c074** | Higher-strength, moderate-elongation bridge | Its alloy family includes a two-stage-aged training example at **1000 MPa, 25% elongation**. Its own aging schedule differs, but it offers promising coverage between c012 and the strength endpoint. |
| **c053** | High-strength anchor | A closely related composition with the same principal heat-treatment temperatures achieved **1380 MPa, 15% elongation**. This is stronger evidence for a useful strength endpoint than choosing several similar high-strength candidates. |

These are **analogue-based selections, not measured pool outcomes**. Together, they target distinct parts of the strength–elongation frontier and avoid concentrating all five picks on one axis.

Final: c018, c051, c012, c074, c053
